title: The Wrong War: Why the Fight for Physical Media Has Become a Toxic Distraction
excerpt: Screaming at developers will not save physical media, but organized action for digital ownership might actually work.
preview: The gaming community is locked in a state of outrage. Since PlayStation announced its plan to move to an all-digital release model in January 2028, social media has been filled with angry posts and community notes.
At first this could have been a unified movement for consumer rights, but instead it devolved into a hate and harassment campaign.

First, we saw influencers disingenuously latch onto the outrage to farm engagement. Small creators took the opportunity to ride the algorithm and grew their followings exponentially in a matter of days. The lack of authenticity became obvious when many of these accounts backpedaled, admitting they would still play the boycotted games and consoles because they needed to do it for their jobs.

This performative outrage fueled a growing wave of online toxicity. The movement is now entirely aimless. If you don’t align perfectly with their anger, you’re immediately attacked. Even early supporters of the boycott who admitted they still wanted to play upcoming massive releases were harassed by anonymous accounts.
bodyHtml:
The gaming community is locked in a state of outrage. Since PlayStation announced its plan to move to an all-digital release model in January 2028, social media has been filled with angry posts and community notes.

At first this could have been a unified movement for consumer rights, but instead it devolved into a hate and harassment campaign.

Influencer Agenda and Aimless Toxicity

First, we saw influencers disingenuously latch onto the outrage to farm engagement. Small creators took the opportunity to ride the algorithm and grew their followings exponentially in a matter of days. The lack of authenticity became obvious when many of these accounts backpedaled, admitting they would still play the boycotted games and consoles because they needed to do it for their jobs.

This performative outrage fueled a growing wave of online toxicity. The movement is now entirely aimless. If you don’t align perfectly with their anger, you’re immediately attacked. Even early supporters of the boycott who admitted they still wanted to play upcoming massive releases were harassed by anonymous accounts.

Denying Facts and Data

The numbers don’t lie.

When the actual market data was released, it proved exactly why physical media is being phased out. We’re entering a phase which started with the film industry, where massive retailers like Best Buy and Target began pulling physical discs from store shelves.

The numbers don’t lie. Modern consumers prioritize convenience over everything else, and digital sales have skyrocketed. Recent U.S. data showed that only seven major games have sold over 100,000 physical copies this year.

Gamers in the community disingenuously attacked this metric making false claims against it and claiming that the post didn’t disclose data that was clearly disclosed. And those who acknowledge the data, but argued against it said “it only accounts for the U.S. sales market”, but that completely ignores the reality. The U.S. is among the two biggest gaming economies, only second to China.

If we factor in China, and their massive footprint in the global gaming economy, the physical data becomes astronomically worse. Physical console media in the Chinese market is practically nonexistent, as their multi-billion-dollar infrastructure is built entirely around digital, PC and mobile distribution.

Instead of accepting reality, parts of the community resorted to spreading misinformation, disinformation and generating fake AI data to counter the facts. We cannot argue with global consumer behavior and smart business decisions nor should anyone bother with disingenuous arguments.

GTA VI Leaks: Who does this hurt?

The most pressing example of this toxic entitlement is the recent Grand Theft Auto 6 leak. Seeing gameplay leak this close to the upcoming Netflix announcement is really disappointing, especially for the devs who put so much work into this.

Some people online claim these leaks are justified because the hacker claims it’s in the name of fighting for physical media, hint: it’s not. But I wonder, who does this strike against corporate greed and decisions actually impact?

As someone who has worked in the gaming industry for 13+ years most recently as a Junior Software Engineer and QA Tester at Sony Interactive Entertainment, I can tell you exactly who this hurts. It does not harm the corporate executives, and it definitely won’t change our inevitable digital-only future. It only hurts and disrespects the developers who have poured years of their lives into developing GTA VI. And, it only ruins the experience for people who have waited years to experience the game spoiler free.

With all this in mind, I question who, how and why would anyone support any of this? There is absolutely zero justification for it.

UPDATE: While writing this article the hacker has made new threats to leak additional content if their demands are not met.

The Real Battle: Digital Rights

Gamers need to mature and shift their focus. Throwing a fit on the internet because the market is changing does not help anyone. We can’t argue with the reality of consumer behavior. The silent majority has clearly already voted with their wallets and digital convenience won.

Not everything is black and white. I don’t want to see physical media disappear. I support having options to choose between physical and digital media. But, if we are rapidly moving into a digital future, we need to focus our energy on something that actually matters.

We should be fighting for concrete digital rights, a true system of digital ownership, and ensuring that the games we buy cannot simply be taken from us.

We can demand better systems without resorting to harassment, and the path for this is through actual legislation. A perfect example of this is happening now through the California with Assembly Bill 1921, also known as the “Protect Our Games Act.”

“When consumers organize legally and push for concrete rights, actual change happens”

The backlash against Ubisoft delisting The Crew, triggered a legislative campaign and it actually passed! This bill was passed by the State Assembly with bipartisan support. How often does that happen?

It imposes strict new rules on publishers, requiring them to provide a two month notice before shutting down a game. It also forces companies to offer solutions, either a playable offline version, a community server patch, or a full refund.

While the current drafted bill only applies to paid digital games released on or after January 1, 2028, it’s a massive step in the right direction. All of this proves that when consumers organize, the right way, legally and push for concrete rights, actual change can happen. Screaming and whining at community managers on social media accomplishes nothing, but passing a state law forces the entire industry to adapt.

A Better Solution: The Right to Archive

I was recently discussing the switch to digital media with a former coworker from PlayStation and I started workshopping a concept to resolve all of this. I believe that if publishers are going to stop providing access to physical media, then the community must be given the legal right and access to archive and print their own.

Building a system where users can back up their digital media to physical devices would be difficult and it definitely opens up a lot of piracy concerns. The complex conversations and new security processes to combat piracy would be a massive undertaking. But, providing a secure method for us to back up our games is only right since the companies want to remove our ability to buy and physical media in the first place.

We can demand true, real digital ownership without toxic hate and harassment campaigns. It’s time we start fighting the right battles.

What are your thoughts on the push for digital ownership? Would you support a legal archiving system if it meant giving up store bought physical discs?

Let me know in the comments below.

Sources:

  • California Legislative Information: Assembly Bill 1921 (Protect Our Games Act) Text

  • Assembly Member Chris Ward: Stop Killing Games just passed a floor vote in California

title: Spider-Man Brand New Day Review
excerpt: Spider-Man: Brand New Day Feels Like a Video Game, and That’s the Highest Compliment I Can Give It
preview: I’ve seen this movie twice now, and that’s the first thing you should probably know, because it’s the thing that surprised me the most. I don’t do that often. I usually see a movie, form my take, and move on to the next one. But Spider-Man: Brand New Day is one of those rare films where I walked out of the theater already thinking about when I was going to go back.

I just got IMAX tickets today, because the IMAX screenings finally opened up. I’m considering Dolby 3D. And I’m still hunting for a ScreenX showing, which I’ll get into, because that’s actually a much bigger story than it sounds like.

Spider-Man: Brand New Day opened at $360 million domestically, and that is the biggest domestic opening weekend in history. It passed Avengers: Endgame, which had $357.1 million, and that’s a record I honestly figured was going to sit there forever.
Worldwide, it pulled $932 million in its opening weekend, which makes it the second biggest global opening of all time behind Endgame‘s $1.223 billion.
bodyHtml:
I’ve seen this movie twice now, and that’s the first thing you should probably know, because it’s the thing that surprised me the most. I don’t do that often. I usually see a movie, form my take, and move on to the next one. But Spider-Man: Brand New Day is one of those rare films where I walked out of the theater already thinking about when I was going to go back.

I just got IMAX tickets today, because the IMAX screenings finally opened up. I’m considering Dolby 3D. And I’m still hunting for a ScreenX showing, which I’ll get into, because that’s actually a much bigger story than it sounds like.

Let’s Talk About the Box Office

Spider-Man: Brand New Day opened at $360 million domestically, and that is the biggest domestic opening weekend in history. It passed Avengers: Endgame, which had $357.1 million, and that’s a record I honestly figured was going to sit there forever.

Worldwide, it pulled $932 million in its opening weekend, which makes it the second biggest global opening of all time behind Endgame‘s $1.223 billion.

I do want to be clear about what these numbers actually are, because opening weekend records and all-time box office records are two very different things. Endgame is still sitting at around $2.79 billion lifetime. Brand New Day has a long way to climb before it’s anywhere near that conversation. But the opening itself is genuinely historic, and the part that impresses me the most isn’t the number. It’s how it happened.

It did all of that without IMAX.

Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey had exclusive rights to IMAX screens in North America for three weekends, which meant Sony was locked out of the biggest premium format in the business during the exact window when a Spider-Man movie needs it most. And The Odyssey wasn’t slowing down either. That film has cleared $911 million after three weekends, and it still took second place this weekend with $51 million. So this wasn’t a case of Spider-Man having the box office to itself. Two enormous movies were running at the same time, and one of them had the premium screens.

Sony broke the domestic opening record anyway.

The ScreenX Thing, Which I Think Is the Real Story Here

Here’s how they got around it, and I think this is the most interesting industry story of the summer.

Sony and CJ 4DPLEX created something called “Shot for ScreenX,” and Brand New Day is the first film in history that was actually shot for the format. That means a second unit was on set during production capturing the footage that plays on the side walls, instead of taking the finished movie and stretching the image out digitally in post. Destin Daniel Cretton has talked about the ScreenX team physically being there on set to shoot those wings.

That’s the IMAX playbook, applied to a format that has spent years being treated as a novelty upcharge on your ticket.

Think about what actually happened there. Nolan spends a decade turning IMAX into a real filmmaker’s format, shoots The Odyssey entirely on IMAX cameras, and locks up the screens. Sony can’t compete on that ground, so instead of just eating the loss, they went and built a rival premium format from the ground up and made their movie the first native release in it.

That’s not a marketing gimmick to me. That’s a studio getting squeezed and responding by creating a new category. And if “Shot for ScreenX” catches on with other filmmakers—and CJ 4DPLEX has said they’re already working with other studios on it—this is going to be the movie that started it.

IMAX has now confirmed that Brand New Day is coming to their screens as The Odyssey‘s exclusivity window closes, and the two films are going to share digital IMAX locations across America. I bought tickets the moment I saw the announcement. I know it’s not true IMAX 70mm, and I’m not going to pretend otherwise. But I still found myself thinking I have to go see this in IMAX, partly to support the movie, and partly because I just want to be in that room again.

The Video Game Thing

Okay, so this is the take that I think a lot of gamers can relate to.

Spider-Man: Brand New Day plays like a video game and feels like Marvel’s first video game adaptation.

It is not officially adapting Insomniac’s Spider-Man or Spider-Man 2. But I sat in that theater for two hours and twenty-five minutes, and I could not stop thinking about those games. Not for a single stretch of the movie. The entire time I was going, “I did that move in this game,” or “I know this reference, I’ve seen this before.”

The way Peter interacts with the police. The traversal. The rhythm of the fights. Even the little things, like the apparel, which is pulled almost directly out of the game in ways that are not subtle at all. If you’ve put twenty hours into those games, you’re going to feel it constantly.

And I mean all of that as a compliment.

Here’s why. Outside of the comics, I think the Insomniac Spider-Man games told the most emotional and the strongest stories in all of modern Spider-Man entertainment. Not only the best action, but yes, the best stories as well. And a big part of that is that those games had twenty-plus hours to build out an expansive world, let the characters breathe, and actually earn their emotional beats. That’s a structural advantage a two-hour movie should never be able to compete with.

Somehow, Brand New Day does the exact same thing in 145 minutes, and I still don’t fully understand how.

Tom Holland has said he was in the writers’ room on this one, and I believe him, because you can feel it in the movie. If you’ve been following his interviews the way I have, he brings up the PlayStation 5 Spider-Man 2 game constantly. He’s an actual gamer. He knows this character. And more than that, he listens to the people who love this character, which is not something you can say about everybody who’s played a comic book role.

So if this ever crosses his feed, I’ll just say this much: Adapt Spider-Man 2. And keep an eye on whatever Insomniac ends up doing with Spider-Man 3.

I also really hope Insomniac Games gets the credit here. You can argue the influence went both directions—that the movies inspired the games and the games inspired the movies—and honestly, the synergy between them is one of the coolest things about all of this. But the DNA of those games is on that screen, and Insomniac built something that genuinely changed how this character moves and feels. A record-breaking movie is now running on that foundation, and I think that deserves to be said out loud.

Is the Movie Overstuffed?

For me personally, the answer is no, and I went in fully expecting it to be.

I felt like I enjoyed every single cast member, and if anything, my complaint runs the other way, because I just wanted more of some of them. If I had to say who this movie is really about, it’s Spider-Man and Punisher. Everything else orbits around those two.

The Hulk material that you saw in the trailer is in there, but it’s a smaller presence than the marketing led me to expect. Ned and MJ are also in it a surprisingly small amount. But none of that is a bad thing. If anything, less is more here. I was happy every time they showed up on screen, and that’s exactly the reaction you want out of an ensemble movie and almost never actually get.

What I appreciated the most is that this movie actually deals with the fallout of No Way Home. Peter is living in a world that doesn’t remember him, and that’s the kind of premise a lot of movies would nod at in the first ten minutes and then quietly walk away from. This one doesn’t. There are real consequences, and it sits in them.

Going into it, I was wondering whether they were going to handle that or dodge it. They handled it, and they handled it well, and I think moving forward the relationships between Peter, MJ, and Ned are going to flourish again in a way that actually feels earned instead of reset.

The MCU Connection, and That Post-Credits Scene

Going into this movie, one of the things I was thinking about most was how connected it was going to be to Doomsday and Secret Wars. Were we going to get a Doctor Doom cameo? Some kind of big setup?

The answer is no, and I think that’s one of the best decisions the movie makes. It’s a really grounded, street-level film that’s confident enough to just be its own thing instead of spending its third act doing homework for the next movie.

The post-credits scene, though. I have to be absolutely honest with you: that is one of the most disappointing post-credits scenes in Marvel history. I felt like I wasted my time sitting there for it. Wait around at your own leisure, but I could have just watched a bad YouTube video about it and lost nothing.

That said, underneath the surface, this movie plants something significant. One of the most important elements of the MCU gets introduced here, and I genuinely think what happens in this film is going to have lasting effects that run through the entire phase after Secret Wars.

When I first saw it, I thought nobody was talking about this. I’ll own that I was wrong there, because three days into wide release everybody is talking about it. What I’ll say instead is that I don’t think people are weighing it correctly yet. There’s a difference between noticing that something happened and understanding what it’s going to cost down the line.

I’m doing a full breakdown and spoiler review of exactly what this means on the channel. Watch the video below, and if you enjoy the coverage, make sure you hit subscribe so you don’t miss the next one!

Seeing It With a Crowd

Both times I saw this movie, the audience was completely locked in.

Not phones out, half paying attention. Actually engaged. Reacting, laughing, applauding. That communal thing that streaming can’t replicate and that people keep announcing is dead.

There was also a pop-up event at the Regal Irvine Spectrum where they gave away posters and shir

ts, plus a photo op with Spider-Man. I got the poster, I missed out on the shirts. All of that footage should be live on my channel right now.

I bring it up because the marketing and the promotion around this release has been a masterclass. Sony didn’t just sell a movie, they built an event around going to see one. I really hope future Marvel movies, and honestly future movies in general, take note of how effective that was, because I think this is going to set the standard for how comic book movies get released going forward.

Rankings, and My Recency Bias

I have to be upfront about something here.

Every time I watch a Spider-Man movie, I realize I have recency bias. I like the most recent Tom Holland Spider-Man movie every single time I see it. The same thing happened with Andrew Garfield, and I told people that at the time. So take everything that follows with that in mind.

Spider-Man isn’t my favorite Marvel character. He never has been. He’s great, and I love seeing him on the big screen, and I get excited every time one of his movies comes out. So for me to now say Spider-Man: Brand New Day is my favorite MCU movie is a big deal.

In terms of Spider-Man specifically, though, my personal favorites are still Into the Spider-Verse and Across the Spider-Verse. Nothing has touched those two for me.

But Brand New Day is now my favorite live-action Spider-Man movie, and I’m including every Sony live-action entry and every MCU Spider-Man film before it. Tom Holland is officially my favorite Spider-Man.

And here’s the part I genuinely did not expect to be typing: I think this might be one of my favorite live-action comic book movies of all time. That means it’s beating out Batman, and I am a crazy Batman fan. It’s beating out Deadpool. If it weren’t for the Spider-Verse movies, I would absolutely be calling this my favorite Spider-Man movie ever made.

I’m going to rewatch the entire franchise and do a proper ranking, because I want to make sure I’m not just riding the high off two viewings in a week. But the fact that I want to go back a third time, and I’m still chasing a ScreenX showing, and I bought IMAX tickets the same day they were announced, tells me something that the numbers can’t.

Where This Leaves Us

We’re four movies into this version of Spider-Man, and it somehow feels like the start of something new.

That’s the strangest and best thing about Brand New Day to me. Sony and Marvel essentially rebooted the Spider-Man franchise without having to recast Spider-Man. The title isn’t just a comics reference; it’s an accurate description of what the movie actually does.

Marvel is having a crazy year. Tom Holland, Zendaya, and Jon Bernthal are all currently starring in two of the biggest movies in the world at the same time, which is an incredible thing to be able to say. Holland is Telemachus in The Odyssey, Zendaya is Athena, Bernthal is Menelaus. Then all three of them turn around and anchor the biggest domestic opening weekend ever recorded.

Doomsday is next, and I’m more excited for it than I’ve been for a Marvel movie in a long time.

Spider-Man: Brand New Day is in theaters now. See it in Dolby, see it in ScreenX, see it in IMAX. Just go see it with a crowd.

I’ll be there again.

title: The Boys Season 5 Episode 5: The Chaos Finally Clicks
excerpt: ⚠️ Spoilers for The Boys Season 5 Episode 5 Titled "One-Shots" below
preview: So yeah… Seth Rogen “died” in The Boys Season 5, Episode 5. Naturally, I thought it’d be hilarious to make a dramatic “in memoriam” post about it. Turns out… not everyone got the joke.

Jokes aside, this episode was actually one of the strongest of the season so far. Instead of sticking to the usual structure, it leans into a chaotic, almost anthology-style format, jumping between different characters across one day.
It’s wild, it’s messy, and it moves fast, but in a good way.
Up until now, the season felt like it was building slowly. This episode changes that. You can feel everything starting to come together heading into the final stretch.
We even get a perspective from Terror, which honestly felt like a deep cut for longtime fans. It’s these kinds of details that make the show stand out even five seasons in.
bodyHtml:
Seth Rogen… RIP 😔 (kind of)

So yeah… Seth Rogen “died” in The Boys Season 5, Episode 5. Naturally, I thought it’d be hilarious to make a dramatic “in memoriam” post about it. Turns out… not everyone got the joke.

Jokes aside, this episode was actually one of the strongest of the season so far. Instead of sticking to the usual structure, it leans into a chaotic, almost anthology-style format, jumping between different characters across one day.

And somehow… it works.

Why the anthology format worked

It’s wild, it’s messy, and it moves fast, but in a good way.

Up until now, the season felt like it was building slowly. This episode changes that. You can feel everything starting to come together heading into the final stretch.

We even get a perspective from Terror, which honestly felt like a deep cut for longtime fans. It’s these kinds of details that make the show stand out even five seasons in.

Is now the time to binge?

If you haven’t started The Boys yet, now’s actually a great time. You’ve got five seasons to binge, plus Gen V, with more spin-offs on the way.

New episodes drop Tuesday night at midnight Pacific Time (technically early Wednesday) on Amazon Prime Video.

If you’re watching this season, I’m curious: what did you think of Episode 5? And if you’re not watching yet… what’s stopping you?

title: Mortal Kombat 2 Review
excerpt: One job… be everything the first Mortal Kombat was not.
preview: To give context, I hated the first Mortal Kombat. So going into this, I had pretty low expectations.

I saw Mortal Kombat 2 early at the premiere, and hype factor aside, I ended up having a really good time with it. This was the first time in a while that I caught myself leaning forward in my seat, cheering, and honestly being a little embarrassed at how into it I was.

The movie starts off in a very similar way to the first one, with something big and exciting that immediately gets the audience hyped. And because of that, I got nervous. The first movie did the exact same thing. It hooked everyone with a great opening, even released that extended intro online, and then completely fell apart.
So once that opening sequence passed, I genuinely thought, “Here we go again.”
But this time, it doesn’t fall off. It keeps the momentum going. It ramps up and just keeps moving.
bodyHtml:
To give context, I hated the first Mortal Kombat. So going into this, I had pretty low expectations.

I saw Mortal Kombat 2 early at the premiere, and hype factor aside, I ended up having a really good time with it. This was the first time in a while that I caught myself leaning forward in my seat, cheering, and honestly being a little embarrassed at how into it I was.

The movie starts off in a very similar way to the first one, with something big and exciting that immediately gets the audience hyped. And because of that, I got nervous. The first movie did the exact same thing. It hooked everyone with a great opening, even released that extended intro online, and then completely fell apart.

So once that opening sequence passed, I genuinely thought, “Here we go again.”

But this time, it doesn’t fall off. It keeps the momentum going. It ramps up and just keeps moving.

What stood out to me the most is that it doesn’t waste time and doesn’t rely on heavy exposition. It introduces Johnny Cage and the rest of the characters quickly, gives you just enough to understand them, and then gets straight into the action.

And that’s where the movie really works. It actually feels like a fighting game.

The structure is simple in the best way. Fights start, they play out, and then we move on. It almost feels like there’s an in-game system pushing things forward. Characters show up, handle what they need to handle, and the movie keeps moving without overcomplicating anything.

At times, it honestly felt like I was watching high-level matches play out in real time, which made the whole experience even more fun.

Another thing I appreciated is that nobody feels safe. There are real stakes, with characters on both sides getting taken out, and it keeps you guessing the entire time. That unpredictability adds a lot to the experience.

It also makes me more interested in where this goes next. If they do a Mortal Kombat 3, there’s a lot of potential to keep building on this.

As for the characters, Cole is definitely improved. He’s handled much better here than he was in the first movie, and he gets exactly what the character needed.

Karl Urban as Johnny Cage is perfect. He fully commits to the role, and it works. I genuinely can’t see anyone else playing this version of the character.

At the screening, I was sitting behind Jack Quaid, and I could hear him reacting during Karl Urban’s scenes. That added to the experience, because you could tell people were really enjoying what he was doing with the character.

Karl Urban just gets it. He understands exactly what Johnny Cage is supposed to be.

Scorpion also has his moment, and it’s still a great one. But unlike the first movie, where he felt like the main focus, here he’s more of a highlight rather than the centerpiece. And honestly, that works better for the overall movie.

If anything, it shows how much stronger the full package is this time around.

Overall, this honestly feels like the blueprint for how fighting game movies should be made. Keep the story simple, focus on the action, and don’t lose sight of what makes the source material fun.

I already posted a full review on YouTube if you want more detailed thoughts, but yeah, this was a fun time.

And if you’re a fan of Mortal Kombat, this is definitely worth watching.

Mortal Kombat 2 arrives exclusively in theaters on May 8th. If you want the full experience, this is a must-see in IMAX! Get your tickets now: Mortal Kombat 2
